solution:
Write the coordination sphere first, then balance the charge with the counter ions.

(i) Cobalt(III) with four \(\text{NH}_3\) and two \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), all neutral, gives a \(3+\) cation, so three chlorides balance it: \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]\text{Cl}_3\)

(ii) Nickel(II) with four \(\text{CN}^-\) gives \(2 - 4 = -2\), so two potassium ions: \(\text{K}_2[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]\)

(iii) Chromium(III) with three neutral en ligands gives a \(3+\) cation: \([\text{Cr}(\text{en})_3]\text{Cl}_3\)

(iv) Platinum(II) with \(\text{NH}_3\) (0), \(\text{Br}^-\), \(\text{Cl}^-\) and \(\text{NO}_2^-\) gives \(2 - 3 = -1\); the '-ate' ending confirms an anion: \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)\text{BrCl}(\text{NO}_2)]^{-}\)

(v) Platinum(IV) with two \(\text{Cl}^-\) and two neutral en gives \(4 - 2 = +2\), balanced by two nitrates: \([\text{PtCl}_2(\text{en})_2](\text{NO}_3)_2\)

(vi) The cation is \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and the anion is \([\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}\); the lowest common multiple of 3 and 4 gives 4 cations to 3 anions: \(\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]_3\)

Name the ligands alphabetically first, then the metal with its oxidation number in Roman numerals; for an anionic complex the metal takes the '-ate' suffix. The oxidation number follows from the charge balance in each case.

(i) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3\), Co is \(+3\): hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride

(ii) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2\), Co is \(+3\): pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride

(iii) \(\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]\), Fe is \(+3\): potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)

(iv) \(\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]\), Fe is \(+3\): potassium trioxalatoferrate(III)

(v) \(\text{K}_2[\text{PdCl}_4]\), Pd is \(+2\): potassium tetrachloridopalladate(II)

(vi) \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}(\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_3)]\text{Cl}\), Pt is \(+2\): diamminechlorido(methanamine)platinum(II) chloride

[Textbook answer-key error in part (iii): the key lists GEOMETRICAL isomerism for \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{NO}_2)](\text{NO}_3)_2\). That complex is of the type \(\text{Ma}_5\text{b}\) — five identical ammine ligands and one nitrito — and in an octahedron every vertex is equivalent to every other, so wherever the single \(\text{NO}_2\) is placed the arrangement is the same one. Geometrical isomerism is impossible for \(\text{Ma}_5\text{b}\); it first becomes possible at \(\text{Ma}_4\text{b}_2\). The isomerism this complex DOES show is linkage (\(-\text{NO}_2\) nitro versus \(-\text{ONO}\) nitrito) and ionisation (nitrite inside the coordination sphere with nitrate outside, or the reverse), which is what the answer below gives. The key's count of possible isomers is not reproducible without the forms it wrongly admits. Parts (i), (ii) and (iv) agree exactly.] (i) \(\text{K}[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_2]\) is an octahedral \([\text{M(AA)}_2\text{B}_2]\) entity, so it shows **geometrical isomerism**: the two aqua ligands may be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans). The cis form has no plane of symmetry, so it also shows **optical isomerism** and exists as a d, l pair; the trans form is achiral.

(ii) \([\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]\text{Cl}_3\) is a tris-chelate \([\text{M(AA)}_3]\) entity. All three didentate ligands are identical and each must span a cis edge, so there is only one geometrical arrangement — no geometrical isomerism. It is chiral, so it shows **optical isomerism** (d and l enantiomers, the two non-superimposable propeller forms).

(iii) \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{NO}_2)](\text{NO}_3)_2\) contains the ambidentate \(\text{NO}_2^-\) ligand, which can bind through nitrogen (\(-\text{NO}_2\), nitrito-N) or through oxygen (\(-\text{ONO}\), nitrito-O), so it shows **linkage isomerism**. The coordinated \(\text{NO}_2^-\) and the counter ion \(\text{NO}_3^-\) can also exchange places, giving \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{NO}_3)](\text{NO}_3)(\text{NO}_2)\), so it shows **ionisation isomerism** as well. Geometrical isomerism is not possible: an \(\text{Ma}_5\text{b}\) octahedron has only one arrangement.

(iv) \([\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)(\text{H}_2\text{O})\text{Cl}_2]\) is square planar of the type \(\text{MABX}_2\), so it shows **geometrical isomerism**: the two chlorides may be cis or trans. Being planar, both forms have a plane of symmetry and neither is optically active.
_note: Types derived from the structure of each entity; the count of every distinct form for (iii) was not enumerated exhaustively, only the isomerism TYPES it exhibits.

solution:
Ionisation isomers differ in which ion is inside the coordination sphere and which is the free counter ion, so they release different ions in water and can be told apart by precipitation tests.

\([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{SO}_4\) has chloride bound to the metal and sulphate free, so in water it gives \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\):

\([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{SO}_4 + \text{Ba}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4\) (white precipitate)

while it gives no precipitate with \(\text{Ag}^{+}\), since its chloride is not free.

\([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{SO}_4)]\text{Cl}\) has sulphate bound and chloride free, so in water it gives \(\text{Cl}^{-}\):

\([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{SO}_4)]\text{Cl} + \text{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \text{AgCl}\) (white precipitate)

while it gives no precipitate with \(\text{Ba}^{2+}\).

The two compounds have the same overall formula but yield different ions in solution and so react differently to the same reagents. That is the evidence that they are ionisation isomers.

In both ions nickel is in the \(+2\) state, so the free ion is \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) with the configuration \(3d^8\) — two unpaired electrons in the free ion. What differs is the field strength of the ligand.

\([\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}\): \(\text{CN}^-\) is a strong field ligand. It forces the two unpaired \(3d\) electrons to pair up, which vacates one \(3d\) orbital. That vacant \(3d\) orbital together with the \(4s\) and two \(4p\) orbitals gives \(dsp^2\) hybridisation, so the ion is square planar. All eight \(d\) electrons are now paired, so there are no unpaired electrons and the ion is diamagnetic.

\([\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}\): \(\text{Cl}^-\) is a weak field ligand and cannot bring about pairing. The \(3d^8\) configuration keeps its two unpaired electrons, no \(3d\) orbital is freed, and hybridisation uses the outer \(4s\) and \(4p\) orbitals — \(sp^3\) — so the ion is tetrahedral. With two unpaired electrons it is paramagnetic, \(\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} = 2.83\,\text{BM}\).

So the square planar cyanido complex is diamagnetic and the tetrahedral chlorido complex is paramagnetic.

The two complexes have the same geometry but different oxidation states of nickel, and that is what decides the magnetic behaviour.

In \([\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}\), nickel is in the \(+2\) oxidation state, so it is \(3d^8\). \(\text{Cl}^-\) is a weak field ligand and does not cause pairing, so two unpaired electrons remain in the \(3d\) set. Hybridisation is \(sp^3\), the ion is tetrahedral, and it is paramagnetic.

In \([\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]\), nickel is in the zero oxidation state, so the atom is \(3d^8 4s^2\). \(\text{CO}\) is a strong field ligand: the two \(4s\) electrons move into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10} 4s^0\), in which every electron is paired. Hybridisation of the empty \(4s\) and \(4p\) orbitals is \(sp^3\), the molecule is tetrahedral, and with no unpaired electrons it is diamagnetic.

So the difference is the oxidation state of nickel and the field strength of the ligand, not the geometry: \([\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}\) is paramagnetic and \([\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]\) is diamagnetic.

In both ions iron is in the \(+3\) state, so the free ion is \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) with the configuration \(3d^5\). The ligands differ in field strength.

\([\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}\): \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is a weak field ligand, so \(\Delta_o\) is less than the pairing energy and the five \(d\) electrons stay unpaired — \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^2\), a high spin, outer orbital \(sp^3d^2\) complex. With five unpaired electrons

\(\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\,\text{BM}\)

so it is strongly paramagnetic.

\([\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}\): \(\text{CN}^-\) is a strong field ligand, so \(\Delta_o\) exceeds the pairing energy and the electrons pair in the lower set — \(t_{2g}^5 e_g^0\), a low spin, inner orbital \(d^2sp^3\) complex. Only one electron is left unpaired, so

\(\mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} = 1.73\,\text{BM}\)

and the ion is only weakly paramagnetic.

An inner orbital complex uses \((n-1)d\) orbitals for hybridisation (\(d^2sp^3\)); an outer orbital complex uses \(nd\) orbitals (\(sp^3d^2\)). Which is possible depends on whether two \(d\) orbitals of the inner set can be emptied.

\([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}\): cobalt is \(+3\), so \(\text{Co}^{3+}\) is \(3d^6\). \(\text{NH}_3\) is strong enough to force pairing, and all six electrons crowd into the three \(t_{2g}\) orbitals. That leaves two \(3d\) orbitals empty, which hybridise with the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals to give \(d^2sp^3\). Because inner \(3d\) orbitals are used, it is an inner orbital (low spin) complex, and with all electrons paired it is diamagnetic.

\([\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}\): nickel is \(+2\), so \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) is \(3d^8\). Even with maximum pairing, eight electrons fill the three \(t_{2g}\) orbitals and still leave two electrons in the \(e_g\) set, so no two \(3d\) orbitals can be vacated. Hybridisation must therefore use the outer \(4d\) orbitals — \(sp^3d^2\) — making it an outer orbital (high spin) complex with two unpaired electrons, and it is paramagnetic.

In \([\text{Pt}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}\) the charge balance is \(x - 4 = -2\), so platinum is in the \(+2\) state and \(\text{Pt}^{2+}\) has the configuration \(5d^8\).

The ion is stated to be square planar, which requires \(dsp^2\) hybridisation. One \(5d\) orbital must therefore be vacant, so the \(5d\) electrons pair up: the eight electrons occupy four \(5d\) orbitals as four pairs, leaving the fifth \(5d\) orbital free for hybridisation with the \(6s\) and two \(6p\) orbitals.

Every \(d\) electron is then paired, so the number of unpaired electrons is

\(n = 0\)

and the ion is diamagnetic, \(\mu = 0\,\text{BM}\).

Both ions contain \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\), which is \(3d^5\), so the difference must come from the crystal field the ligands produce. In an octahedral field the \(d\) orbitals split into the lower \(t_{2g}\) set and the upper \(e_g\) set, separated by \(\Delta_o\), and the configuration adopted depends on \(\Delta_o\) compared with the pairing energy \(P\).

In the hexaaqua ion \([\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\), \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is a weak field ligand, so \(\Delta_o < P\). It costs less to place an electron in the upper \(e_g\) set than to pair it, so the five electrons spread out singly as \(t_{2g}^3 e_g^2\) — a high spin configuration with **five unpaired electrons**.

In the hexacyanido ion \([\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}\), \(\text{CN}^-\) is a strong field ligand, so \(\Delta_o > P\). Pairing now costs less than promotion, so the electrons fill the lower set first as \(t_{2g}^5 e_g^0\) — a low spin configuration with **one unpaired electron**.

Hence the aqua complex has five unpaired electrons and the cyanido complex only one.
